--- title: "Data Visualization" description: "Standard visualizations for EDA, matplotlib and seaborn fundamentals, variable-based formatting, and multiplotting with FacetGrid." author: "John Robin Inston" date: "2026-05-06" date-modified: "2026-05-06" toc: true title-block-banner: false page-navigation: true execute: echo: true --- ::: {.callout-important title="Learning Objectives"} - Understand what exploratory data analysis (EDA) is and how visualization supports it. - Know which plot types to use for univariate, bivariate, and grouped data. - Produce scatter plots, bar plots, histograms, box plots, and violin plots in `matplotlib` and `seaborn`. - Apply variable-based formatting (color, shape, size) to encode additional dimensions. - Create multiplots using `matplotlib` subplots and `seaborn` FacetGrid. ::: ## Exploratory Data Analysis ### What is EDA? After acquiring and preparing data, the next step in the data science lifecycle is [exploration]{.accent}. ::: {.callout-important title="Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)"} **Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)** is the process of analysing and visualising data to understand its structure, identify patterns, and uncover insights. ::: EDA typically follows three steps: 1. **Univariate analysis** — understand the distribution of individual variables. 2. **Multivariate analysis** — explore relationships between variables. 3. **Insight development** — form hypotheses to inform modelling and deeper analysis. ![EDA Workflow](../assets/images/eda_workflow.svg) A key tool throughout EDA is [data visualization]{.accent}. Python's standard library does not include a full visualization system, so we use dedicated libraries: `matplotlib`, `seaborn`, `altair`, and `plotly`. ### Why Visualize Data? Visualization helps to: - Improve [interpretability]{.accent} of data. - Identify [patterns and relationships]{.accent} that are not obvious in raw tables. - [Communicate]{.accent} findings effectively to an audience. - Explore data in an [interactive]{.accent} way. Aim for visualizations that are: - **Novel** — contribute something beyond a plain table. - **Informative** — answer a specific question. - **Efficient** — convey the message with minimum ink. - **Aesthetic** — clear and visually appealing. > Always ask yourself: what is this visualization for? What is it contributing? ### Types of Visualization Typically we wish to produce visualizations for two main reasons: - **Exploratory visualizations** — created quickly during analysis to understand the data; not necessarily polished. - **Presentation visualizations** — used to communicate findings; refined with a focus on clarity and aesthetics. Furthermore, we can categorize visualizations by their level of interactivity: - **Static** — fixed images; no user interaction. - **Interactive** — allow zooming, filtering, and hovering for detail. - **Animated** — show changes in data over time or across conditions. ## Visualization Libraries ### `matplotlib` The foundational visualization library in Python. Almost every other library — including `seaborn` — is built on top of it. - **Imperative** interface: total control over all plot details, but often verbose for common plots. - Strong for fine-grained customization and publication-style figures. - We use the **object-oriented interface** (`fig, ax = plt.subplots()`), which is more flexible than the pyplot state-based interface. ### `seaborn` A **declarative** statistical visualization library built on top of `matplotlib`, similar to `ggplot2` in R. - Creates common statistical visualizations with much less code. - Provides useful defaults for themes, color palettes, and grouped comparisons. - Well suited for EDA and rapid iteration. ## Standard Visualizations We use the `penguins` dataset from `seaborn`, which contains measurements of penguins from three species: Adelie, Chinstrap, and Gentoo. ::: {#a2d221e9 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} penguins = sns.load_dataset("penguins") print(penguins.shape) penguins.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (344, 7) ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}
species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g sex
0 Adelie Torgersen 39.1 18.7 181.0 3750.0 Male
1 Adelie Torgersen 39.5 17.4 186.0 3800.0 Female
2 Adelie Torgersen 40.3 18.0 195.0 3250.0 Female
3 Adelie Torgersen NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN
4 Adelie Torgersen 36.7 19.3 193.0 3450.0 Female
``` ::: ::: ### Scatter Plots A **scatter plot** pairs two continuous variables to visualise their relationship. We can produce a scater plot in `matplotlib` by calling `ax.scatter()` on an axis object: ::: {#416b9d94 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5)) ax.scatter( "bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", data=penguins, color="steelblue", alpha=0.95, s=7, marker="D" ) ax.set( xlabel="Bill Length (mm)", ylabel="Bill Depth (mm)", title="Penguin Bill Length vs Depth" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Scatter plot of bill length vs bill depth (matplotlib).](data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=585 height=449 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: We can produce the same plot in `seaborn` with less code by calling `sns.scatterplot()`: ::: {#da2b4a44 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid", palette="Set2") ax = sns.scatterplot( x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", data=penguins ) ax.set( xlabel="Bill Length (mm)", ylabel="Bill Depth (mm)", title="Penguin Bill Length vs Depth" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Scatter plot of bill length vs bill depth (seaborn).](data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-5-output-1.png){width=589 height=455 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: #### Variable-Based Formatting To examine the influence of a **third categorical variable**, we can map it to the color (`hue`), shape (`style`), or size (`size`) of points. ::: {#53d73c74 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = sns.scatterplot( x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", data=penguins, hue="species" ) ax.set( xlabel="Bill Length (mm)", ylabel="Bill Depth (mm)", title="Penguin Bill Length vs Depth" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Scatter plot colored by species (seaborn).](data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-6-output-1.png){width=589 height=455 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ### Bar Plots A **bar plot** represents categorical data with rectangular bars whose lengths are proportional to the values they represent. They are commonly used to show counts or proportions across categories. In `matplotlib`, we need to pre-aggregate the data before plotting. ::: {#9012bdcc .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} bp1_data = penguins.groupby("species").size().reset_index(name="count") print(bp1_data) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` species count 0 Adelie 152 1 Chinstrap 68 2 Gentoo 124 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#b401cc75 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5)) ax.bar(x="species", height="count", data=bp1_data, color="steelblue") ax.set(xlabel="Species", ylabel="Count", title="Penguin Species Counts") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Bar plot of species counts (matplotlib).](data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-8-output-1.png){width=597 height=455 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: #### Count Plots In `seaborn` to avoid the initial aggregation we can use `countplot` which computes category counts automatically: ::: {#5885e3e2 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = sns.countplot( x="species", data=penguins ) ax.set( xlabel="Species", ylabel="Count", title="Penguin Species Counts") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Count plot of species (seaborn).](data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){width=597 height=455 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: #### Subgrouping To compare across two categorical variables, use the `hue` parameter to split each bar into subgroups. ::: {#4ed3a640 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = sns.countplot(x="island", hue="species", data=penguins) ax.set(xlabel="Island", ylabel="Count", title="Penguin Species Counts by Island") ax.legend(title="Species") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Species counts by island with subgrouping by species (seaborn).](data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){width=597 height=455 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ### Box Plots A **box plot** (box-and-whisker plot) displays the distribution of a continuous variable using the five-number summary: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, and maximum. Outliers are shown as individual points. ::: {#05dac8fb .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = sns.boxplot(x="species", y="bill_length_mm", data=penguins) ax.set( xlabel="Species", ylabel="Bill Length (mm)", title="Penguin Bill Length by Species" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Box plot of bill length by species (seaborn).](data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.png){width=589 height=455 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ### Histograms A **histogram** groups continuous data into bins and represents the frequency of observations in each bin as a bar height. ::: {#82b17716 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = sns.histplot(x="bill_length_mm", data=penguins, bins=20) ax.set(xlabel="Bill Length (mm)", ylabel="Frequency", title="Histogram of Penguin Bill Length") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Histogram of bill length (seaborn).](data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-12-output-1.png){width=589 height=455 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: #### Histograms with Kernel Density Estimates Setting `kde=True` overlays a **kernel density estimate (KDE)** — a smooth approximation of the distribution. Combined with `hue`, we can compare distributions across groups in a single plot. ::: {.callout-note} Histogram shape depends on bin count and KDE smoothness depends on bandwidth. Use these as exploratory summaries rather than definitive descriptions of the distribution. ::: ::: {#e73cca47 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = sns.histplot( x="bill_length_mm", data=penguins, bins=20, kde=True, hue="species", multiple="layer" ) ax.set(xlabel="Bill Length (mm)", ylabel="Frequency", title="Histogram of Penguin Bill Length") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Histogram with KDE curves by species (seaborn).](data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-13-output-1.png){width=589 height=455 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ### Violin Plots A **violin plot** combines a box plot with a KDE, providing a richer view of the distribution's shape, central tendency, and spread. ::: {#2f0831a7 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = sns.violinplot( x="species", y="bill_length_mm", data=penguins, inner="quartile", color="steelblue" ) ax.set( xlabel="Species", ylabel="Bill Length (mm)", title="Penguin Bill Length by Species" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Violin plot of bill length by species (seaborn).](data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-14-output-1.png){width=589 height=455 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ## More Advanced Visualizations ### Creative Combinations Don't treat plot types as rigid categories — effective visualizations often layer multiple geometries. For example, overlaying individual data points on a box plot reveals both the summary statistics and the raw distribution. ::: {#481ae0e9 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = sns.boxplot( x="bill_length_mm", y="species", data=penguins, color="lightsteelblue" ) sns.stripplot( x="bill_length_mm", y="species", data=penguins, color="black", alpha=0.5, size=4, ax=ax ) ax.set( xlabel="Bill Length (mm)", ylabel="Species", title="Penguin Bill Length by Species" ) plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Box plot with strip plot overlay (seaborn).](data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-15-output-1.png){width=635 height=455 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ### Encoding Continuous Variables We can map a continuous variable such as body mass to point size using the `size` and `sizes` parameters. ::: {#4e47b82e .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} ax = sns.scatterplot( x="bill_length_mm", y="bill_depth_mm", data=penguins, hue="species", style="species", size="body_mass_g", sizes=(20, 200), alpha=0.7 ) ax.set( xlabel="Bill Length (mm)", ylabel="Bill Depth (mm)", title="Penguin Bill Length vs Depth Scaled by Body Mass" ) ax.legend(title="Species") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Scatter plot encoding species (color, shape) and body mass (size) (seaborn).](data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-16-output-1.png){width=589 height=455 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ## Multiplotting ### Multiple Plots with `matplotlib` `plt.subplots()` creates a figure with multiple axes. We then loop through axes to apply a plot to each subset of data. ::: {#c2964a3a .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows=1, ncols=3, figsize=(15, 5)) species = penguins["species"].unique() for ax, sp in zip(axes, species): subset = penguins[penguins["species"] == sp] ax.scatter( subset["bill_length_mm"], subset["bill_depth_mm"], color="steelblue", alpha=0.95, s=7, marker="D" ) ax.set_title(sp) ax.set_xlabel("Bill Length (mm)") ax.set_ylabel("Bill Depth (mm)") plt.tight_layout() plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Per-species scatter plots using matplotlib subplots.](data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-17-output-1.png){width=1428 height=463 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: ### Facet Grids with `seaborn` `sns.FacetGrid()` produces the same result with far less code. It creates a grid of subplots defined by the unique values of one or more categorical variables; `g.map()` applies a plotting function to each facet. ::: {#35b9d5be .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = sns.FacetGrid(penguins, col="species", height=4, aspect=1) g.map(sns.scatterplot, "bill_length_mm", "bill_depth_mm", color="steelblue", alpha=0.95, s=7, marker="D") g.set_axis_labels("Bill Length (mm)", "Bill Depth (mm)") g.fig.subplots_adjust(top=0.8) g.fig.suptitle("Penguin Bill Length vs Depth by Species") plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Per-species scatter plots using seaborn FacetGrid.](data-visualization_files/figure-html/cell-18-output-1.png){width=1136 height=377 fig-align='center'} ::: ::: `FacetGrid` is particularly powerful for EDA because it scales to many groups with no additional code — simply change the `col`, `row`, or `hue` arguments.
